chapters.title: Chapter 3: Calculating and Paying Advance Tax

lessons.title: Estimating Your Annual Income and Tax Liability

body.text: Advance tax is calculated on an estimate, and nobody expects the estimate to be perfect. The law asks for a reasonable figure in June, and lets you correct it in September, December and March. A good estimator is not someone who predicts the year. It is someone who revises on time.

children.text: Every advance tax payment starts with one number: your estimated tax for the whole tax year. Get it badly wrong and you either pay interest or park money with the government that you could have used. This lesson gives you a practical method, head by head, and then follows one taxpayer as she revises her estimate through the year.
What the Law Asks You to Do

markDefs.definition: Your best estimate, at the time of each instalment, of your total income for the entire current tax year, including income not yet received.

children.text: Section 405 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (old section 209) tells you to compute advance tax on your

for the tax year: apply the rates in force, subtract any rebate and relief, and subtract TDS and TCS you expect. You do not file the estimate anywhere. It lives in your own worksheet, and the only evidence of it is the challans you pay.

body.latex: \text{Advance tax} = \text{Tax on estimated income for the full year} - \text{Rebate and relief} - \text{Expected TDS and TCS}
body.caption: Recalculate this before each due date

children.text: Building the Estimate Head by Head
Income tax sorts income into five heads, and each one is best estimated in a different way. The trick is to use hard data where you have it and cautious assumptions where you do not.

body.caption: How to estimate each head of income

cells: Annual CTC components, plus known bonus; ignore bonuses that are not confirmed
Rent from a let-out flat or shop
Monthly rent × months let out in the year, less 30% standard deduction and municipal taxes paid
Freelance fees, consulting, F&O and intraday trading
Profit so far plus confirmed work in the pipeline; for presumptive taxpayers, 50% or 6% to 8% of expected receipts
Invoices, bank statements, broker P&L, accounting app
Share and mutual fund sales, property sale
Gains already booked, plus sales you have definitely decided to make; do not guess future market gains
Broker tax P&L, CAMS or KFintech capital gains statement
FD and savings interest, dividends, family pension
Deposit amount × interest rate for the year; dividends already received plus announced dividends

body.caption: Annualising works for steady income such as rent or a regular retainer. It does not work for lumpy income such as capital gains or project fees

body.title: Quick Check: Pick the Right Method
body.question: It is early June. Nikhil, a salaried taxpayer in Kolkata, sold shares for a ₹1,40,000 short-term gain in May. What should his June advance tax estimate assume for capital gains for the full year?
options: ₹1,40,000 × 12 ÷ 2 = ₹8,40,000, annualising the gain from April and May
₹1,40,000, the gain already booked, plus any sales he has definitely decided to make
Nothing, because capital gains are unpredictable and can be ignored until March
A guess based on where he expects the Nifty to be in March
body.explanation: Capital gains are lumpy, so annualising them makes no sense. The sensible estimate is what is already booked, plus sales already planned. He should not ignore the booked gain: it exists on 15 June, so tax on it belongs in the June instalment. Gains that arise later can be added when they happen, and the relief for capital gains protects him from interest on earlier instalments.

children.text: Following One Estimate Through the Year

Aditi is a 33-year-old product designer in Gurugram on the new regime. Her salary is ₹24,00,000, and her employer's TDS of ₹2,92,500 covers it exactly. She also freelances for two overseas clients with no TDS, and holds ₹14 lakh in FDs earning about ₹1 lakh a year, with 10% TDS.

cells: Less TDS on salary and FD

body.title: Aditi's estimated advance tax for the year, at each due date
Show me the math: Aditi's September estimate

children.text: Slab income is salary after standard deduction (₹23,25,000) plus freelance profit (₹5,00,000) plus FD interest (₹1,00,000), which is ₹29,25,000. Slab tax is ₹3,00,000 on the first ₹24 lakh plus 30% of ₹5,25,000 (₹1,57,500), totalling ₹4,57,500. The short-term gain adds 20% of ₹2,00,000, which is ₹40,000.

content.caption: Total tax with cess, in rupees

children.text: Subtract TDS of ₹3,02,500 (salary ₹2,92,500 plus ₹10,000 on FD interest) to get estimated advance tax of ₹2,14,900. By 15 September, 45% of that, ₹96,705, must have been paid. She has already paid ₹16,635, so she pays ₹80,070 on this date.

Three things stand out. First, each instalment is calculated on the latest estimate, not the June one. Second, the September jump is mostly the August share sale, and because that gain arose after 15 June, the capital gains relief means no interest for having left it out of the June payment. Third, her March figure came in slightly below December, so her last payment simply shrank. Estimates can go down as well as up.

body.title: Try It: The September Top-Up
body.prompt: In June, Harish in Bhopal estimated advance tax for the year at ₹1,20,000 and paid 15%, which was ₹18,000. In September, his estimate is unchanged at ₹1,20,000. How much must he pay on or before 15 September? Answer in rupees.
body.explanation: By 15 September, 45% of ₹1,20,000 must have been paid cumulatively, which is ₹54,000. He has already paid ₹18,000, so he pays ₹36,000 on this date. If his estimate had risen, the 45% would be applied to the new, higher figure.

children.text: Which Regime Should the Estimate Use?

Your estimate should use the regime you will actually choose when you file. The new regime is the default. Salaried taxpayers without business income can still pick the old regime each year when filing, but anyone with business or professional income faces restrictions on switching back and forth. For most people the new regime now produces lower tax, but not for everyone.

body.title: Karthik, Coimbatore: ₹15 lakh salary, estimated both ways

columns.label: Old regime
points: Section 80C investments ₹1,50,000, health insurance ₹25,000, home loan interest ₹2,00,000

children.text: Even with ₹3,75,000 of deductions, Karthik pays ₹42,900 less under the new regime. If his employer deducted TDS under the old regime because that is what he declared in April, his salary TDS would be higher than his real tax, and his advance tax estimate would need to reflect that difference.

body.text: Surcharge rarely matters for this course's audience, but know where it starts. Under the new regime a surcharge of 10% applies when income exceeds ₹50 lakh, 15% above ₹1 crore and 25% above ₹2 crore, with marginal relief at each step. On short-term and long-term gains from listed shares and on dividends, surcharge is capped at 15%. If your estimate is close to ₹50 lakh, include it.

children.text: Should You Estimate High or Low?

stats.label: Cost of underpaying
stats.context: Simple interest for deferring instalments or not paying enough, equal to 12% a year

stats.label: Earned on an excess refund
stats.context: Interest paid by the department on refunds of excess advance tax, generally from 1 April after the tax year

stats.label: Maximum cost of a low June guess
stats.context: Interest on each instalment shortfall runs only until the next due date, if you catch up then

children.text: The asymmetry favours estimating slightly high. Underpaying costs more than overpaying earns, and a refund comes back with interest. But the penalty for a cautious early estimate is also limited, because interest for a short instalment runs for three months, not the whole year, provided you catch up at the next due date.

body.title: Scenario: Vikas and a Blockbuster Quarter
body.scenario: Vikas is a full-time F&O trader in Ahmedabad with no other income, on the new regime. By 12 June 2026 his net F&O profit for the year is ₹9 lakh, an unusually strong start. If he simply multiplies by four, he gets ₹36 lakh for the year. His more cautious estimate, allowing for losing months, is ₹18 lakh.
body.prompt: Which estimate should he use for the June instalment? What does the choice cost him if the year really does end at ₹36 lakh, assuming he catches up in September?
body.modelAnswer: A ₹36 lakh estimate implies tax of ₹6,86,400 and a June instalment of ₹1,02,960. An ₹18 lakh estimate implies tax of ₹1,66,400 and a June instalment of ₹24,960. Trading profit is volatile and SEBI data shows most traders give back gains, so multiplying one good quarter by four is not a reasonable estimate. The cautious ₹18 lakh is defensible. If the year does end at ₹36 lakh and he raises his estimate and catches up to 45% by 15 September, the extra cost of the low June payment is interest at 1% a month for three months on the ₹78,000 shortfall, which is ₹2,340. That is a small, bounded price for not locking up ₹78,000 of trading capital on a guess. Note that F&O profit is business income, so the capital gains relief does not apply, and the September catch-up really matters: the longer he waits, the more instalments carry interest.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The Computation Section
body.textWithBlank: The section of the Income-tax Act, 2025 that tells you how to compute advance tax on estimated current income is section ___.
body.explanation: Section 405 carries forward old section 209. It is read with section 404 (the ₹10,000 threshold) and section 408 (the instalment dates and percentages).

body.title: Build Your Estimate in 30 Minutes
steps: Open a spreadsheet with one row for each income source and one column for each due date: June, September, December, March
Fill in salary and pension from your CTC or payslips, and rent from your agreement
Add FD interest as deposit × rate, and check AIS for interest and dividends already reported
Add capital gains already booked from your broker or CAMS statement, and only sales you have decided on
Add business or freelance profit to date plus confirmed work, or presumptive income on expected receipts
Compute tax under the regime you will choose, subtract expected TDS and TCS, and apply the cumulative percentage for the next due date
Before every due date, overwrite the previous column with fresh figures rather than editing old ones, so you can see how the estimate moved

body.label: Income and Tax Calculator: Income Tax Department
body.description: Use the official calculator to sanity-check your estimated tax under both regimes before each instalment.

cards.definition: Your best estimate, at each due date, of total income for the whole tax year, including income not yet received.
Tells you to compute advance tax on estimated current income at the rates in force, less rebate, relief, TDS and TCS.
Scaling income so far to a full year. Suitable for steady income like rent, not for lumpy capital gains or project fees.
Recalculating before each due date and applying the cumulative percentage to the latest estimate, not the original one.
10% above ₹50 lakh, 15% above ₹1 crore, 25% above ₹2 crore, capped at 15% on listed equity gains and dividends.
Underpaying costs 1% a month; excess tax refunded earns 0.5% a month. A slightly high estimate is usually cheaper.

points: Advance tax is based on an estimate of the full year's income, recalculated before each due date
Estimate each head differently: salary and rent from contracts, interest from deposits, capital gains from what is already booked, business income from profit to date plus confirmed work
Apply each cumulative percentage to your latest estimate and pay only the difference from what you have already paid
Use the regime you will actually choose; for most taxpayers the new regime now gives lower tax
Underpaying costs 1% a month while refunds earn 0.5% a month, so err slightly high, but a cautious early estimate costs little if you catch up promptly
Keep a dated worksheet so every revision, up or down, is visible and defensible

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax, legal or investment advice. Section references are to the Income-tax Act, 2025, with the corresponding Income-tax Act, 1961 section in brackets. Examples use rates, deductions and surcharge thresholds for tax year 2026-27 as understood at the time of writing, which can change with each Union Budget. Verify current rules or consult a qualified chartered accountant before acting.
